title: Shortest Way to Form String
statement:
A subsequence of a string is what remains after deleting any number of its characters (possibly none) while keeping the others in their original order.

Given two strings `source` and `target`, find the smallest number of subsequences of `source` that, written one after another, spell exactly `target`. The same `source` may be used as many times as needed, each time choosing a new subsequence. Return that number, or `-1` if `target` cannot be built this way.
constraints: source and target contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Each subsequence of `source` covers a contiguous chunk of `target`, so the question is how to cut `target` into as few chunks as possible, each of which is a subsequence of `source`. A brute force tries every cut with dynamic programming. The greedy shortcut: always make the current chunk as long as possible. A longer first chunk leaves a shorter rest of `target`, and a suffix of a string never needs more chunks than the whole, so being greedy never costs an extra piece.

Making a chunk as long as possible is just the "is subsequence" check with two pointers: walk through `source` once and advance in `target` whenever the letters match.

## Approach

1. Keep `j`, the next letter of `target` to cover, and `count`, the chunks used.
2. While `j` has not reached the end, remember `start = j` and scan `source` with `i`, moving `j` forward each time `source[i]` equals `target[j]`.
3. If the scan did not move `j`, the letter `target[j]` does not occur in `source`, so return `-1`.
4. Otherwise one more chunk was used; add 1 to `count` and repeat.
5. Return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`source = "abc"`, `target = "abcbc"`. The first scan matches `a`, `b` and `c`, so `j` goes from 0 to 3 and `count = 1`. The second scan skips `a` (it wants `b`), then matches `b` and `c`, so `j` reaches 5 and `count = 2`. All of `target` is covered, so the answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(S·T): every scan of `source` costs O(S) and covers at least one letter of `target`.
- Space: O(1) besides the input.

## Pitfalls

- Without the `j === start` check, a letter missing from `source` makes the loop run forever.
- Stop the inner scan once `j` reaches the end of `target`, or `target[j]` reads past it.
- Count a chunk only after a scan that matched something.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | subsequences of `source` used so far |
| `j` | index of the next letter of `target` to cover |
| `start` | value of `j` when the current scan began |
| `i` | position in `source` during a scan |

narration.2: No subsequence of source has been used yet.
narration.3: j points at the first letter of target still to be covered.
narration.4: Keep building chunks until all of target is covered.
narration.5: Remember where this chunk starts, to see whether the scan makes progress.
narration.6: Walk through source once, stopping early if target is finished.
narration.7: This letter of source matches the next letter target needs...
narration.8: ...so take it and move on in target.
narration.11: The scan matched nothing: target[j] never appears in source.
narration.12: So target cannot be formed at all.
narration.14: The scan used one more subsequence of source.
narration.16: All of target is covered; return the number of subsequences used.
